# 2 Maccabees Chapter 3 — The EMET Bible (Literal)

**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 3 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_003_page_001.jpg

---

**1** While the holy city was inhabited with all peace and the laws were still being maintained very well because of the piety of Onias the high priest and his hatred of wickedness,

**2** it came about that even the kings themselves honored the place and glorified the temple with the finest presents,

**3** so that even Seleucus the king of Asia defrayed from his own revenues all the costs pertaining to the service of the sacrifices.

**4** But a man named Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin, who had been made administrator of the temple, came into conflict with the high priest about the regulation of the market in the city.

**5** When he could not prevail over Onias, he went to Apollonius, the son of Thraseas, who at that time was governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia.

**6** He reported to him that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of untold sums of money, so that the total amount of the funds was beyond counting, and that they did not belong to the account of the sacrifices but that it was possible for them to fall under the authority of the king.

**7** When Apollonius met the king, he told him about the money he had been informed of. The king selected Heliodorus, who was in charge of his affairs, and sent him with commands to carry out the removal of the aforesaid money.

**8** Heliodorus set out at once, ostensibly to make a tour of inspection of the cities of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, but in fact to carry out the king's purpose.

**9** When he arrived at Jerusalem and had been courteously received by the high priest of the city, he told him of the information that had been given and revealed the purpose for which he had come, and he inquired whether this was in fact so.

**10** The high priest explained that there were deposits of widows and orphans,

**11** and also some money belonging to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, a man of very prominent position, and that the total came to four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. To those who had put their trust in the sanctity of the place and in the dignity and inviolability of a temple honored throughout the whole world, wrong could not possibly be done.

**12** But Heliodorus, because of the king's commands, said that the money must in any case be confiscated for the royal treasury.

**13** So he set a date and went in to direct the inspection of these funds. There was no small distress throughout the whole city.

**14** The priests prostrated themselves before the altar in their priestly garments and called toward heaven upon him who had given the law about deposits, that he should keep them safe for those who had deposited them.

**15** To see the appearance of the high priest was to be wounded at heart, for his face and the change of color disclosed the inward agony of his soul.

**16** For terror and bodily trembling had come over the man, which plainly showed to those who looked at him the pain lodged in his heart.

**17** People hurried out of their houses in crowds to make a general supplication because the holy place was about to be brought into contempt.

**18** Women, girded with sackcloth below their breasts, thronged the streets. Some of the virgins who were kept indoors ran together to the gates, and some to the walls, while others peered out of the windows.

**19** And all, stretching forth their hands toward heaven, made supplication.

**20** There was something pitiable in the prostration of the whole multitude and in the anxiety of the high priest in his great agony.

**21** While they were calling upon the Almighty LORD to keep what had been entrusted to those who had entrusted it in full safety, Heliodorus carried out his purpose.

**22** But just when Heliodorus arrived with his bodyguard at the treasury, the Sovereign of spirits and all authority caused so great a manifestation that all who had dared to accompany him, struck by the power of God, became faint and terrified.

**23** For there appeared to them a horse with a terrifying rider, adorned with very beautiful trappings, and it rushed furiously and struck Heliodorus with its front hooves, and its rider seemed to be arrayed in golden armor.

**24** Moreover, two other young men appeared to him, exceedingly strong and surpassingly beautiful, with glory surrounding them. They stood on either side of him and flogged him continuously, inflicting many blows upon him.

**25** Heliodorus fell suddenly to the ground and was enveloped in great darkness. His men picked him up, put him in a litter,

**26** and carried him away — this man who had just entered the aforesaid treasury with a great retinue and all his bodyguard but was now unable to help himself. They clearly recognized the sovereign power of God.

**27** While he lay prostrate, speechless because of the divine intervention and deprived of any hope of recovery,

**28** they praised the LORD who had acted marvelously for his own holy place. And the temple, which a little while before was full of fear and disturbance, was filled with joy and gladness, now that the Almighty LORD had appeared.

**29** Then some of Heliodorus's friends quickly begged Onias to call upon the Most High to grant life to one who was lying quite at his last gasp.

**30** So the high priest, suspecting that the king might get the impression that some foul play had been perpetrated by the Jews with regard to Heliodorus, offered a sacrifice for the man's recovery.

**31** While the high priest was making the atoning sacrifice, the same young men appeared again to Heliodorus dressed in the same clothes, and they stood and said, "Be very grateful to Onias the high priest, since it is for his sake that the LORD has granted you your life.

**32** And you, having been scourged from heaven, report to all men the majestic power of God." Having said this they vanished.

**33** So Heliodorus offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made very great vows to the Savior of his life, and having bidden Onias farewell, he marched off with his forces to the king.

**34** And he bore testimony to all men of the deeds of the supreme God which he had seen with his own eyes.

**35** When the king asked Heliodorus what sort of person would be suitable to be sent once more to Jerusalem, he replied,

**36** "If you have any enemy or plotter against the government, send him there and you will get him back well flogged, if he indeed escape with his life, for there is truly some power of God about the place.

**37** For he who has his dwelling in heaven watches over that place himself and brings it aid, and those who come to do it injury he strikes and destroys."

**38** Thus the affairs of Heliodorus and the keeping of the treasury turned out this way.
